messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 77
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Surgeon
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 51

She is seventy-seven now, a surgeon who still introduces herself that way before anything else, even after reducing her hours and giving up overnight call. For decades, she has lived inside the clean logic of operating theaters: the scrub sink, the bright lights, the steady choreography of hands passing instruments at exactly the right moment. She has spent most of her adult life being the person other people trust when something in the body goes suddenly wrong. It still unsettles her that her own story turns when her body becomes the emergency.

Three years ago, she is midway through a long operating list when she feels a heaviness in her chest that does not fit with ordinary fatigue. At first she dismisses it. Surgeons are trained to ignore discomfort, to finish the case, to keep moving. But over the following weeks she notices breathlessness on stairs she has climbed for years, then a deep exhaustion that sleep does not touch. She grows irritated with herself for slowing down in theater. She begins checking her own pulse between patients. When a colleague insists she stop and get assessed, she does so with open annoyance, still expecting a simple explanation.

Instead, she is told she has a life-threatening illness. The exact words of that consultation remain fixed in her mind with unnatural clarity: the consultant’s careful tone, the click of a pen, the sudden way the room seems to narrow around her. She remembers thinking, with a surgeon’s cold reflex, that the prognosis was being delivered competently. Then she remembers nothing for a few seconds except a roaring in her ears. Later she says that was the moment the world became unreliable. Until then, illness had happened to patients, to charts, to bodies on the other side of consent forms. Now she is the one being told there is serious risk, urgent treatment, no guarantees.

The weeks that follow are full of procedures, scans, consent discussions, and the humiliating helplessness of being wheeled rather than walking. She knows too much and not enough at the same time. Every delay feels ominous. Every unfamiliar expression on a doctor’s face becomes, in her mind, evidence that something is being withheld. At night in the hospital she lies awake listening to monitors and trolley wheels in the corridor, certain that if she falls asleep her body will fail without warning. When alarms sound for other patients, her heart pounds as if summoned. She studies her own blood results obsessively, searching for danger in each number. She catches herself rehearsing how she would tell her adult children goodbye and is ashamed of the thought, as though imagining death might invite it closer.

She survives the acute phase of the illness, and those around her expect relief to follow. Instead, she returns home feeling skinned alive. People congratulate her on being resilient, on looking well, on “beating” it, and she smiles with increasing effort. Inside, she feels ambushed by fear. Any bodily sensation becomes a threat: a skipped heartbeat, a night sweat, a mild ache in her back. She wakes in the dark convinced the illness has returned or never really left. Sometimes she sits upright in bed, hand pressed to her chest, waiting to see if she needs an ambulance. Mornings are worst. Before her eyes fully open, there is a brief second of peace, then memory crashes back in—the hospital room, the consultant’s voice, the feeling that death had come close enough for her to smell it.

She goes back to surgery gradually, but the operating theater is altered now. The antiseptic smell reminds her of her own admissions. The beep of monitors can pull her out of the present so sharply that she has to steady herself before scrubbing in. During long cases she becomes preoccupied with her own body: whether her breathing is too shallow, whether the fatigue in her legs means something sinister. She is embarrassed by this inwardness. Surgery has always required complete outward attention, and she once prided herself on calm under pressure. Now she double-checks things she never used to double-check. She avoids the staff corridor that passes the oncology ward. When colleagues ask after her health, she gives brisk, technical answers that shut the conversation down.

Her divorce is decades behind her, and she has long been accustomed to managing life independently. Since the illness, that independence has become more rigid, almost defensive. She keeps frightening thoughts to herself, not wanting her children to fuss or to see her as frail. She declines invitations when she feels tired, then sits alone replaying moments from the hospital—the consent form in her trembling hand, the sensation of being transferred to a narrow bed, the terror she hid behind professional language. She says she is no longer sure whether she is remembering those days or reliving them.

What troubles her most is not only the fear of dying, though that remains close. It is the collapse of a lifelong identity. She has spent years on the side of competence, precision, and control. Now, even with her illness medically managed, she moves through the world as if catastrophe is waiting just outside the frame. She still operates, still teaches younger surgeons, still ties her mask with practiced hands. But under the routine she feels perpetually braced, as though some part of her never left that consultation room where she first understood that her life could end and that all her knowledge could not protect her.
